2881.summary:
This is a process paper, not a treasury paper. It sets out when the 2027/28 budget will be scrutinised and approved, not what is in it. There are no borrowing figures, no prudential indicators and no treasury position — the capital programme is described only as being funded partly by "application of external borrowing", with no amount.

One number does matter. The council is carrying a funding gap of £13.659m in 2027/28, rising to £27.524m by 2029/30 — it roughly doubles over three years, against a General Fund net budget of £437m. And 65% of that budget (£281.8m) sits in three demand-led services the report itself identifies as the most volatile.

We would not send a member email for this meeting. There is nothing here a councillor could usefully challenge on treasury grounds, and a manufactured question would spend credibility we will want for the meetings that deserve it.
2881.no_email_reason: Process and timeline paper with no treasury content. The budget substance arrives at the December Executive; that is the meeting worth writing to.

36189.summary:
The 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy Statement, adopted by Full Council on 19 February 2026. Standard Arlingclose-drafted shape. The book at 31 December 2025 is £422.598m of external debt at 3.13% weighted — PWLB £380.598m at 3.01%, LOBOs £32.000m at 4.34%, other loans £10.000m at 3.89% — plus £34.066m of PFI and leases. Investments £154.152m at 4.26%.

Two things in the paper are worth writing to about. First, every one of the £32m of LOBOs has its option window in 2026/27, and the paper itself acknowledges the probability of a call: 'with long-term interest rates having risen in recent years, there is now a good chance that lenders will exercise their options' (para 3.19). Twelve LOBO calls across nine councils in our library have all been refused; this is the only book we have read where every remaining LOBO comes callable in a single 12-month window.

Second, the balance-sheet trajectory. Internal borrowing runs from £152.4m (31.3.25) to £282.0m (31.3.29) — an 85% rise — while investments fall from £137.963m to negative £27.005m. The liability benchmark (Table 2) reaches £422.0m by 31.3.28 against a projected external position of £406.0m the same year: the point at which internal borrowing runs out. Strategy (para 3.11) is deliberate — favour short-term and internal over new long-term fixed while short rates are still expected to fall.

Balance-sheet identity CFR − external borrowing − other long-term liabilities = internal borrowing closes to £0.001m rounding across all five years of Table 1.

Loan-book reconciliation against our file did not tie — see internal block — so no loan-book claim appears in the email.

summary.text: The 2026/27 strategy is deliberate and clearly written. The distinctive fact for outreach is that all £32m of the LOBO book has options during 2026/27 and the strategy names the probability that lenders will exercise. That is the hook the email is built on, because the cross-council pattern — twelve calls, nine councils, twelve refused — is something no single authority can see from its own book. Second layer is the balance-sheet trajectory: internal borrowing 85% higher over four years and the liability benchmark closing on external by 31 March 2028. Loan-book reconciliation against our PWLB file did not tie exactly (see internal); no loan-book claim goes in the email.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 strategy that went to Full Council on 19 February, six months in. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

We wrote because of paragraph 3.19.

All £32m of your LOBOs have their option windows during 2026/27, and your own strategy names the reason — with long-term rates having risen, there is a good chance lenders will exercise. Yours is the only book we have read where every remaining LOBO comes callable inside a single twelve-month window, and what we have on how the sector has been handling those calls is probably the most useful thing we can offer you before the dates arrive.

Twelve calls so far, across nine councils. Every single one refused, and the loan repaid or refinanced. Not one authority in our file has accepted the new rate. The largest was Harrow's £20.8m — their last remaining LOBO, called, declined and repaid, funded with £65m of new PWLB. Wolverhampton is the one council that published the actual offered rates alongside the originals: three loans at 3.60%, 4.26% and 4.29% offered new terms of 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26%, all rejected, described in their own report as "deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted". Dexia is on the other side of six of the LOBO books we hold. Your paper doesn't name the counterparty, so we can't say from here whether you sit inside that pattern — but the direction of the sector is one you cannot see from any single book.

A sector-wide refusal rate of twelve out of twelve says the option is worth very little at current rates, which is presumably why lenders exercise at all — no single council can assemble that count from its own papers, which is why we publish it. For context on what the alternatives cost, pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows the whole sector's monthly PWLB draws by rate and maturity, and on this afternoon's certainty rates (PWLB notice 314/26 PM, 14 August), one year sits at 4.95%, five at 5.34%, ten at 5.83% and twenty at 6.38%.

One other observation from Table 1, offered as an observation rather than anything more. Your internal borrowing runs from £152.4m to £282.0m over the four years to 31 March 2029 — an 85% rise, deliberately taken because paragraph 3.11 favours internal and short-term over new long-term fixed while short rates are still expected to fall. The liability benchmark in Table 2 reaches £422.0m by 31 March 2028 against a projected external position of £406.0m the same year: the point on your own numbers at which internal borrowing runs out and external has to take over. The pathway is interactive at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark and updates against live rates, which is worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes.

On training, four fit North Northamptonshire. Alternatives to PWLB covers LOBOs and what the sector's call record now looks like. Strategic PWLB borrowing goes to the certainty-versus-HRA-rate question and the timing choice between fix-now, forward-start and short. The liability benchmark pathway covers Table 2. And Interest rate risk, since your indicator caps the three-year revenue impact of a 1% move at £6.675m either way. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
